en: May that indescribable dark-blue splendor, whose limbs are naturally beautiful and who is the object of Lakṣmī’s affection, grant you auspiciousness. This is the first chapter.
Whose two feet bear the grace of the morning lotus, with the Ganges' shimmering waves dancing upon the matted locks of Shiva who bows before them.

I worship that form of the Lord Bharga, which is a jewel that brings joy to the eyes of beautiful women, the abode of the seven-fold prosperity, possessing eighteen clearly manifest arms, and which is to be partaken by me, its devotee,
as it is produced within the vessel-like womb of the jar during the course of the hour.
A hundred verses, intent upon rivaling the nectar of a woman’s lower lip.
By the grace of Divākara and with the desire for the health of the sick,
we shall briefly compose this excellent poem, the *Vaidyajīvana*.
Nevertheless, this treatise is composed; for even though there are wicked people, the world does not behave as if it were full of wretchedness out of fear of bandits.
Those whose minds are not attached to women,
nor immersed in the ocean of the nectar of literature—
will they ever understand my efforts?
Just as the charms of a courtesan are [useless] to the blind.
I shall indeed write down the entire secret of that which was taught out of compassion for humanity by the sages such as Caraka and others, who were skilled in the eradication of disease.
There is nothing here that has been fabricated by one's own imagination.
Having studied the entire science of medicine under his guru, possessing the nectar in his hands, skilled in medical procedures,
free from worldly desire, steadfast in courage, and compassionate.
A physician who is pure and qualified should be such as this.
First, one should determine the nature of the disease according to the rules for diagnosis;
thereafter, the physician should examine whether it is curable and then proceed with treatment.
Let those afflicted by fever abandon the medicine of foolish physicians,
just as virtuous men avoid a wife who is attached to contact with others.

If wholesome conduct exists for one afflicted by disease, what is the use of employing medicine? If wholesome conduct does not exist for one afflicted by disease, what is the use of employing medicine?

Just as the masses of water from the ocean were taken up by the clouds, so too was the milk accepted by the royal physicians for the lotus-feet of Mahīndra’s queen, which had been made to blush with shame.
Even though it was naturally tasteless, it was taken up by those physicians for the king.
The Sarasvatī will become full of aesthetic flavor for the Lord of Murāśā.
O fawn-eyed one, at the very first encounter with her beloved, the wise woman will experience exhaustion here, but thereafter she shall experience great bliss.
Just as a householder who has newly taken up the [nine] vows.
Since fever is generally the most powerful among all diseases,
we shall therefore provide its remedy first.
O lady with beautiful breasts, one should first drink a digestive decoction of *devadāru*, *dhanvana*, and the two types of *bṛhatī* during a fever.
With *chinnaruhā*, *uśīra*, *musta*, and *dhanvayāsa*;
with *kirātatikta*, *musta*, *reṇukā*, and *yāsa*;
and with *viśva*, *vṛṣa*, *musta*, and *dhanvayāsa*.
The decoction [is used] in fevers caused by wind, bile, and phlegm.
One afflicted by a fever born of Vāta should drink this decoction prepared from uśīra, kalaśī, mahauṣadha, kirātatiktaka, āmbhodhara, sthirā, the two types of bṛhatī, amṛtalatā, and trikaṇṭa.
The man [is seen] by you whose eyes have the tips of their lashes like the petals of a thousand-petaled lotus.
O beloved, drinking this decoction of the feet of the Pīyūṣaloka-pañcālīs destroys the fever of Hanumān’s father.
A decoction prepared from *chinnodbhava*, *aparpaṭa*, *vārivāha*, *bhūnimba*,
and *śuṇṭhī* [is beneficial] for those shattered by fevers born of wind and bile.
Indeed, the "Five-Auspicious" brings about what is truly auspicious.
Indeed, a single decoction made from *parpaṭaka*, combined with sandalwood water and great medicinal herbs, truly destroys bile-born fever.
If that is so, what need is there for further deliberation?
The water decoction of *drākṣā*, *parpaṭa*, *rājavṛkṣaka*, *kaṭukā*, *mustā*,
and *abhayā* is used for fever caused by pitta characterized by fainting, emaciation, heat, thirst, delirium, and confusion; likewise,
[the decoction] derived from *duḥsparśā*, *pramadā*, *kirātatiktaka*, *kaṭukā*, *siṃhāsya*, and *reṇukā*.
This decoction, when combined with sugar, removes thirst, burning sensations, hemorrhagic disorders, and fevers caused by blood and bile.
Aha! For what purpose were so many decoctions prescribed by sages such as Parāśara and others,
when [the goal] is severed merely by drinking water infused with *aśivā* and *parpaṭa*?
Why does the fever born of bile not spread?

This sixfold [remedy], joined with the water-born (lotus), the water-born (lotus-seed), the dust of the clouds (camphor), and the universal medicine (sandalwood)— cooling and providing immediate relief— is always effective against burning heat.
This should be administered for fever and thirst, even in the case of acute fever.
A decoction of red sandalwood, padmaka, dhānyaka, chinnaruhā,
and picumanda [is used] for fever arising from pitta and kapha, burning sensations, and thirst.
He would be the remover of the fire that destroys one's vomited [food].
The fever of the maker, who yearns for union with another woman, bears the thinness of one anointed with ghee purified a thousand times.
Just as there is desire for one's own wives.
Thirst, burning fever, and delusion are pacified by applying a foam made from the shoots of the *nimba* tree,
just as the wealth of wealthy men [is increased].
From the company of courtesans.
With pure lotuses, with languid breezes, and with flower-nectars combined,
they were filled with curiosity for the story of their water-sports.
It may even conquer the ailments born of bile-fever.
Of those beautiful women, whose vine-like bodies were adorned with sandalwood paste, whose expansive breasts were covered with pearls,
and whose words were charming with clever wit.
Embracing dispels all burning heat.
A bed fashioned from sprouts and lotus petals; clothing [provided] by companions together with friends in the forest among excellent trees shimmering with flowers; singing accompanied by the lute;
conversations composed of parrots, ruddy geese, and cuckoos; and most lovely, endearing stories.
And breezes produced by fans of pure palm leaves dispel the burning heat.
O lady of shapely hips, eager for song, sweet-voiced one, utterly languid with passion—
upon your body, which is filled with the heat of love, coolness has been applied.
An ointment made from snow, moonbeams, and water.
Sleeping in a palace that bears the splendor of white clouds, as beautiful as the rays of the moon, and anointed with sandalwood, dispels all suffering.

O you who are dearer than life, let not men distressed by bilious fever drink the water of various creepers with hanging fruit, which brings only despair when drunk. O lord of physicians, what can they do? O charming one, enjoy yourself in happiness.
The beloved's lip alone instantly removes all torment and is sweeter than nectar.
"O physician, tell me what medicine there is for those burnt by the side-glances of their beloveds?
A firm embrace is the beneficial diet, and the kiss of the lower lip is the medicinal decoction."
In a fever caused by bile, what is the use of meat-broths, cold infusions, or medicinal pastes; or what is the use of decoctions, or even nectar?
Only the face of one's beloved is to be drunk.
It was constantly experienced by Lolimbarāja.
Morning rice-water that has stood overnight, when drunk mixed with sugar,
removes internal burning pain, just as the worship of Durgā removes suffering.
A decoction prepared from the five roots (pañcamūla), amṛtā, mustā, viśva,
bhūnimba, and sādhita quickly pacifies fever arising from wind (vāyu).
An electuary (avaleha) prepared from śṛṅgī, kaṇā, kaṭphala, and puṣkara, combined with honey,
is prescribed for one afflicted by phlegm along with asthma and cough.
One shall conquer fever here; there is no doubt whatsoever.
A decoction made from bhārṅgī, guḍūcī, ghanasāra, dāruharidrā, siṃhī, śuṇṭhī, pippalī,
and puṣkaramūla destroys fever and alleviates asthma.
It produces hunger and extends one's appetite.
Two things cause me wonder: that this bitter and astringent [juice] destroys the bitterness of the mouth, and that it has been pressed from the lotus-bud of her breast.
The woman attains abundant joy.
A decoction made from *kaṭphala*, *kaṭtṛṇa*, *abda*, *dhanikā*, *śṛṅgī*, *ugragandhā*, *abhayā*, *bhārṅgī*, *parpaṭa*, *viśva*, and *devataru*, combined with *bāhlīka* and *madhu*,
cures cough, dyspnea, diseases of the mouth, fever, and the provocation of *balāsakapha*.
In the same way, O lady of tender throat, it also removes the pain produced in the throat.
O slender one, a citron flower with filaments, smeared with ghee and powdered rock salt,
cuts away your lack of appetite and brings back your desire for the lotus.
Her eye, which puts the wagtail to shame, is just like that.
Of granthi, indrajā, amarapuṣpā, kṛmighna,
bhārṅgī, bhṛṅgī, trikaṭu, anala, kaṭphala, pauṣkara, rāsnā, abhayā, the two types of bṛhatī, dīpyaka, and bhūtakeśī—
Of the female Keśinī, Kirātaka, Kavaca, Cavi, and Vṛkī.
This decoction destroys all types of *saṃnipāta* disorders,
confusion of the intellect, perspiration, coldness, and delirium; it also cures colic, flatulence, abscesses, and disorders of phlegm and wind.
Likewise, [it is used] for those suffering from wind-diseases and for women who have recently given birth.
There is no difference whatsoever in the timing of a fatal encounter;
therefore, who is more powerful than the physician who conquers it?
O delighter of the wise, tell me: what indeed should not be given to that mine of compassion who rescues those submerged in the ocean of the [three] humors' confluence?
He who can liberate one seized by the python of the three humors is the king of physicians;
even his own self should be given to him, let alone gold and other riches.
The swelling arising from the root of the ear that occurs when the fever born of the three *doṣas* has subsided is hard; in that case, one should remove blood with leeches,
and the patient should drink clarified butter prepared with equal parts of *rāsnā*, *nāgara*, the root of *luṅga*, *hutabhuj* (*citraka*), *dārvī*, and *agnimantha*.
O lady with eyes worthy of worship by the lotus, this ointment shall destroy swelling and pain.
A decoction of arka, anantā, kirāta, amarataru, rasajā, sindhuvāra, ugragandhā, tarkārī, śigru, the five pungents (pañcoṣaṇa), ghuṇadayitā,
and mārkava immediately removes severe disorders of the three humors (tridoṣa), as well as "bow-wind" (dhanurmāruta) and lockjaw (dantabandha).
It causes intense coldness in the limbs, labored breathing, coughing, and diseases of the wind (vāta) associated with childbirth.
A decoction prepared from *tikta*, *atiktaka*, *parpaṭā*, *amṛtā*, *śaṭī*, *rāsnā*, *kaṇā*, *pauṣkara*, *trāyantī*, *bṛhatī*, *surauṣadhi*, *śivā*, *duḥsparśā*,
and *bhārgī* destroys the accumulation of the three *doṣas*, as well as daytime sleepiness and insomnia.
At night, it [removes] thirst, dryness of the mouth, burning sensations, cough, and asthma—all of them without exception.
A person who drinks milk boiled with the five roots (pañcamūla) shall be freed from colic located in the flanks and head, from cough, from dyspnea, and from chronic fever.
This single preparation of jaggery and long pepper (guḍapippalī) conquers chronic fever and the ailments of indigestion.
What need is there for other medicines for loss of appetite, indigestion, aversion to food, jaundice, parasites, vomiting, and dyspnea?
A decoction of *chinnodbhava* (guḍūcī) combined with *kaṇā* (pippalī) destroys chronic fever accompanied by phlegm,
just as Rāma destroyed the ten-faced Rāvaṇa and Balarāma destroyed Pralamba.
Just as Rāma [conquered] Kārtavīrya at the forefront of battle.
By the consumption of a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūlī) together with black pepper,
chronic fever arising from phlegm (kapha) flees.
This decoction, prepared from these nine ingredients— śaṭī, śuṇṭhī, reṇukā, surataru, anantā, bṛhatī, musta, tiktā, and indeed tiktaka—
and mixed with honey and sugar, when drunk, pacifies [the fever].
It completely eliminates the three doshas, even when they are irregular, as well as chronic fever.
A decoction made from vāsā, paṭola, triphalā, drākṣā, śamyāka, and nimba,
taken with honey and sugar, destroys quotidian fever (ekāhika-jvara).
"O slender-limbed one, alas, some wretched man who was childless has died on the banks of the northern shore of the Ganges;
let someone offer him a handful of water."
He would be your younger brother for only a single day.
This decoction is accompanied by camphor, sugar, great medicinal herbs,
nalada, kaṇa, and payodhara;
it is likewise joined with honey and sugar.
Victory to the third eye, O fawn-eyed one!
One afflicted by a quartan fever is cured by nasal drops (nasya) consisting of aged ginger mixed with clarified butter;
likewise, one gains the favor of playful women in the bloom of their youth.
Goodness [arises] as if from the mere sight of the face.

To alleviate quartan fever, one should administer a nasal drop made from the leaves of the *munidruma* tree mixed with water, which is equal in brilliance to the unblemished moon of the autumn season.
A decoction boiled with *suradāru*, *śivā*, *aśivā*, *sthirā*, *vṛṣa*, and *viśva*,
combined with honey and sugar.
When fully drunk, it will pacify quartan fever.

Afflicted by the cold, one should consume buttermilk mixed with the powder of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), or likewise wine; or one should use a *kambalarallaka* woolen blanket or a horse-blanket (*kuthā*). Then, women languid from the pride of youth should embrace him firmly until the frost has passed.
The fawn-eyed women, whose full breasts were smeared with saffron from Kashmir, were at their pleasure.
A decoction of śakra, āhva, dāru, ghana, vṛṣa, amṛtā, nirguṇḍikā, bhṛṅga, mahauṣadha, along with kṣudrā and yavānī.
The sacrificial fire for the forest of cold fevers.
The *amṛtalatā* (nectar-creeper), which surpasses nectar with the sweetness of its speech; *lakṣmīśivābhā* (resembling Lakṣmī and Śivā) and *śivā* (auspicious);
*viśvavarā* (the best in the universe) and *ghanakucā* (with firm breasts), by whom the universe is pervaded; and *siṃhī* (the lioness) with a lion-like belly (*siṃhodarī*).
A decoction prepared from these five medicinal herbs, combined with *madhuka* (liquorice) and *kaṇā* (long pepper), [is effective].
If the irregular fever is yellow, O slender-limbed one, why then does it not diminish?
The decoction of *sanāgarā*, *sapayodharā*,
*sasiṃhikā*, and *saguḍūcikā* mixed with honey [is used as] a nursing-mother's decoction.
Mixed with Kaṇā, it destroys irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
There are no other venerable medicines,
O beloved; indeed, there is no other application superior to a paste of garlic combined with oil.
Even in the case of a great wind-disorder or a remittent fever.
Cetakī mixed with honey becomes a destroyer of poison; Pippalī taken in increasing doses destroys poison;
and Ajājī combined with jaggery destroys irregular pains.
When consumed with jaggery, it pacifies even such fierce [diseases].
Why do you, my beloved, wave this blue water-lily with both hands? Listen to these words of mine, which are like the essence of nectar—
words that act as the *kulaka-nimba-siṃhīndra-jā* for the chronic fever of worldly existence.
Having destroyed the impurities of the afflictions, it flows abundantly joined with honey.
O you whose luster surpasses the sun, whose eyes are tremulous, whose braided hair shines with a mass of *mālatī* flowers, O you with a belly like that of the five-faced one!
[O you who possess] *paṭola*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *madhuka*, *cetakī*, and *mustaka*...
One who has prepared a decoction quickly overcomes a disorderly [disease].
O you with breasts like golden jars, whoever should worship her who is dark as honey,
for him there shall never be any afflictions from the god of love.
O charming one, abandon even a moment’s agitation;
O slender one, listen to my words with attention:
He dwells at the foot of the Meghanāda tree upon my head.
O wide-eyed one, it becomes exceedingly difficult to traverse.
This decoction, sweet as honey, removes the bitterness of *amṛtā*, *aśivā*, and other [bitter herbs],
just as I remove your anger, O proud lady.
Rolling forcefully at her lotus-like feet.
O delicate one, whose body is a jewel of lotus-glow, whose lotus-eyes are tremulous, who holds the essence of desire—
may the nectar-cloud of Śiva bring me joy amidst this adversity.
O you who delight in the playful sport of the uneven one, the god whose arrows are uneven!
O you of intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, O mind of the wise, exceedingly slow in the face of the god of love!

[This is] the fever-alleviating [remedy] consisting of *rug*, *ariṣṭa*, *śivā*, *vacā*— The final portion of the verse is incomplete in the provided text. Based on the context of classical Sanskrit medical (Āyurvedic) literature, the missing words likely refer to medicinal herbs used to cure fever (*jvara*). A probable completion might be: ... *vaca-śatāvarī-śarkarā-samprayuktam idam auṣadham*. Thus, the full translation would be: "O you of intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, O mind of the wise, exceedingly slow in the face of the god of love! This medicine, composed of *rug*, *ariṣṭa*, *śivā*, *vacā*, *śatāvarī*, and sugar, is the remover of fever."
Incense made from barley, sacrificial offerings, lac, and mustard seeds.
A decoction prepared from *tikta*, *uśīra*, *balā*, *dhānya*, *parpaṭa*,
and *ambhodhara* quickly wards off a fever that has returned again.
Ghee prepared with *gopīdvyā*, *āmalakī*, *sthirā*, *magadhajā* (long pepper), *tiktā*, milk, *pālinī*, *drākṣā*, *śrīphala*, *dhāvanī*, *hima*, *viṣā*, *mustā*,
and *indrajā* (vaca) cures irregular fevers, consumption, pain in the head and sides, and loss of appetite.
The blossom-cluster of the play-vine pacifies vomiting, emaciation, and chlorosis.
Service to trees swaying in the wind, fire-offerings with mantras, worship of the three-eyed Lord Śiva, the twice-born, and one's guru, the recitation of a thousand names of Viṣṇu,
wearing jewels, acts of charity, and the blessings of ascetics— [all these are rendered fruitless].
This entire [work] clearly sets forth the eight fevers along with their fatal signs (ariṣṭa).
O jewel-like girl, O treasury of arts, O you with a voice as tender as a cuckoo’s,
is he possessed by fever or free from fever?
One should take a light meal at the end of the day.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fever," in the *Vaidyajīvana* composed by Lolimbarāja, son of Śrī Divākara. The second chapter begins with *amṛtātiviṣāsurarājayava-* (Guduchi, Ativisha, Devadaru, and barley...).
Listen, O lady with breasts like the frontal globes of a conquered elephant, to [the description of] stanayitnu, kirātaka, viśva, and payas, which remove diarrhea and destroy fever.

A decoction prepared with *śīta*, *uśīra*, the two types of *yugma*, *vatsaka*, *vṛkī*, *padmāhvā*, *dhānyā*, *amṛtā*, *bhūnimba*, *ambuda*, *bāla*, *bilvaka*, *ativiṣā*, and *viśva*, when sweetened with honey,
overcomes nausea, thirst, and vomiting.
It is effective against burning sensations, loss of appetite, constipation, and diarrhea, and it overcomes all types of dysentery and fever.
With *pañcāṅghri*, *vṛkī*, *abdabala*, *indrabīja*, *tvakṣevya*, *tikta*, *amṛta*, *viśva*, and *bilva*,
[one cures] fevers and dysenteries along with vomiting and coughs.
The decoction pacifies asthma and pain.
In cases of a predominance of phlegm, or a predominance of wind, or a predominance of both, the heavy pañcamūla should be used;
in a predominance of bile, the light pañcamūla should be used.
Why do you ask again and again, O deer-eyed one?
This decoction is declared to consist of devadāru, viṣa, pāṭhā,
jantuśatru, ghana, tīkṣṇa,
and vatsaka.
Born from the jar of the ocean during an epidemic of swelling and dysentery.
O dear one, for those who cherish Murāri with love,
what need is there for children, wealth, grain, or all the world?
For even he [the Lord] is not subject to the affliction of dysentery.
What is the use of the splendor of children, abundant grain, or the entire world?
Diarrhea caused by bile is cured by rice-water mixed with bilva and musta;
who here, other than you, O wise one, could know the remedy?
This powder of *indrajā*, *meghamada*, *kusumaśrī*, *lodhra*, *mahauṣadha*, and *mocarasa*, combined with jaggery and buttermilk—
It quickly cures severe diarrhea.
O auspicious one, you whose slender body is as graceful as a golden creeper, O lovely lady with a face like a ripe paddy ear, listen: [there are] ginger,
madana-fruit, flowers, resin of the moca-tree, and ajamoda.
Combined with buttermilk, they pacify even severe diarrhea.
The Śyāmā plant, which pacifies dysentery, is adorned with variegated leaves;
it bestows growth upon those with weak digestion and shines like the night.
Victorious is she who possesses feet, hands, and lips like the young sprouts of the *bāla* creeper;
whose breasts are like hills adorned with garlands of jasmine; who wears a girdle blazing with jewels;
who is encircled by shimmering earrings; and who is endowed with a red lotus and a trident.
A decoction prepared from *tīsāra*, *kuṭaja*, *abdalva*, *bilvaka*, *viṣā*, and *dīpya* [is used].

This great [preparation] named Gaṅgādhara is prepared from equal parts of dhātakī, āmalakī, payodhara, vṛkī, kaṭvaṅga, yaṣṭīmadhu, the fruit-pits of śrījambu and āmra, nāgara, viṣā, hrīvera, lodhra, and indraja, along with rice-water.
This powder quickly removes all chronic diarrhea; it is supreme.
O you whose breasts strike the ball, O you who take away the intoxication of the pride of feminine beauty! You are a dyer [red] during the flow of blood.
The barks of the *samadhu*, pomegranate, and *vatsaka* [are used].
Sandalwood mixed with pure rice-water, combined with honey and sugar,
destroys thirst and destroys [the excess of] blood.
It causes emaciation and excessive urinary excretion.

One should consume *bilva* together with jaggery to destroy abdominal pain and pain from indigestion (*āmashūla*), and to conquer various types of hemorrhage and dysentery; [this should be done] when the breasts are as large as a *bilva* fruit.
One suffering from thirst, dyspnea, cough, fever, swelling, fainting, hiccups,
aversion to food, vomiting, and colic, as well as one afflicted with diarrhea,
should forcefully recite [this mantra].
"Govinda, Gopāla, Gadādhara!"
Jatiphala, nagara, sarpa-phenau,
and khārjūra-phala— this [mixture] should always be used, two niṣkas each, along with [the ash] produced from dried cow dung.
And everything produced in the forest is equal to ashes.
A physician should administer this twice daily, in a dose of only half a niṣka, with the wash-water of *śubha* rice,
in cases of chronic diarrhea accompanied by blood.
It is beneficial when accompanied by pain and characterized by great force.
Yavānī, nāgara, uśīra, dhanikā, ativiṣā, ghanā,
bālabilva, and dviparṇī constitute a digestive stimulant (dīpana) and a digestive aid (pācana).
A decoction prepared from punarnavā, bāṇapuṅkha,
viśvā, agni, pathyā, cirabilva,
and bilva pacifies all [diseases] without exception.
[It cures] diseases of the spleen, abdominal tumors, and disorders of the digestive tract.

A decoction made from equal parts of ginger (śuṇṭhī), chinnaruhā, viṣā, and jaladhara is beneficial even in cases of chronic dysentery (grahaṇī) accompanied by the presence of undigested matter (sāma), when the digestive fire is weak.
For one who drinks ghee boiled with a paste of ginger, it removes anemia (pāṇḍu) and cough.
There may be a downward movement of wind, and the digestive fire moves with force.
A powder made from *pāṭhā*, *viṣā*, the bark of the fruit of *kuṭaja*, *abhayā*, *tiktā*, *madana*, *rāsnā*, *nāgara*, and *bilva*,
taken with honey and rice-water, cures *grahaṇī* and diarrhea.
One should administer it in cases of rectal pain caused by a flow of blood and in diseases arising from the rectum.
Equal parts of *kirātatikta*, *kaṭukā*, *mustā*, *indrayava*, and *tryūṣaṇa*; one part each of *candrakalā* and *kuṭaja*; and two parts of *citraka*.
This powder, named *Ratnakalā*, when combined with jaggery and milk, [cures] anemia and fever.
It cures dysentery, loss of appetite, jaundice, abdominal disorders, gulma, and urinary disorders.
A powder should be prepared from equal parts of kṣāra, dvandva, paṭu, trika, trikaṭuka, cavyā, ajamodā, nala, kṛṣṇā, mūlaka, hiṅgu, jīra, and miśi;
it should be drunk with lukewarm water, the juice of *kola*, or with buttermilk, along with other medicinal substances.
It is generally beneficial for heart disease, hunger, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, sprouts of disease, and disorders of the large intestine, especially when it is dear to one's beloved.
A bolus of jaggery (guḍa) combined with the two alkalis, the six pungent spices, asafoetida, and ajamodā, along with the single juice of sal tree resin,
citron, and jujube, is highly recommended for disorders of phlegm and wind, as well as for dyspepsia.
O you whose face is the chief of constellations, you are fully capable of illuminating and ripening.
A powder prepared from *cavya*, *kaṭukā*, *śrī*, and *viśvabheṣaja*,
when taken with buttermilk, destroys the painful *grahaṇī* disorder.
Powdered rucaka, agni, and marīca, when consumed with buttermilk (takra),
destroys disorders of the digestive tract, abdominal enlargements, tumors, hemorrhoids, loss of appetite, and splenic enlargement.
Ghee that is well-cooked with a paste of *payodhara*, *jala*, *indrajā*, *bālaka*, *bilva*, *hrībera*, and *mocarasa*,
yet accompanied by the persistence of rawness (*āma*) and mixed with blood;
It immediately cures disorders of the digestive tract in a housewife.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Grahaṇī*," in the *Vaidyajīvana* composed by Lolimbarāja, son of the illustrious Divākara.
Hereafter begins the third chapter, O lady of tender speech, concerning cough—
We shall now describe the remedy for dyspnea:
a decoction prepared from the heavy *pañcamūla* (the five roots) together with *capalā* (cinnamon) cures cough.
O beautiful woman, this pill, produced from *ghanaviśva*, *śivā*, and molasses, when held within the lotus of the mouth for three days,
removes asthma and cough.
Like a lover, she is placed within the heart as if it were snow.
One hundred palas of goat’s urine and one hundred palas of *kalidruma* (mālatī) boiled together with honey quickly cures cough.
And likewise, one should treat labored breathing and balāsa (phlegm) in the same manner.

Take half a *tula* of *ārdraka* (ginger), half that amount of jaggery (*guḍa*), and likewise half a portion each of cumin (*kustumbarī*), *dīpyaka*, *āyojaraṇa*, the three aromatics (*trijātaka*), and black pepper (*jalada*). One should cook these ingredients according to the proper method; this linctus (*leha*) called *Ratnakala* has been described by me for you alone, my beloved.
It destroys cough, hemorrhoids, fever, catarrh, swelling, pain, abdominal tumors, and consumption.
The powder of rāsnā, balā, padmaka, devadāru, the three fruits (triphalā), the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa),
and vella, combined with honey and ghee, is a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
It dispels both labored breathing and coughing.
With a decoction of vāsā, haridrā, dhanikā, guḍūcī,
bhārṅgī, kaṇā, nāgara, and dhāvanī,
combined with the dust of mārīca;
Whose breaths would not go to destruction? No man's.
The quantities of clove, black pepper, nutmeg, and cinnamon bark should be equal;
the heartwood of khadira is said to be equal to all of these together;
and this powder is combined with a decoction made from the babbuḷa tree.
This pill cures coughs when taken at the end of eight ghaṭikās.
Crushing the wind, swallowing the phlegm, uprooting chronic rhinitis, clarifying the vision, strengthening the luster, dispelling heart disease,
completely pacifying abdominal ailments, and kindling the digestive fire.
This universal decoction is known as the means for dispelling cough and dyspnea.
"O lotus-faced one, what is the nature of *rūpa*? What is the vocative case of the word for 'mountain' (*nṛ*)? What is the sixth vowel of the seed-syllable of fire (*agnibīja*)?
Whose decoction is it?"—thus was she questioned by her beloved.
Worthy of homage from the learned, she quickly gave this reply to the Nāgara.
As long as molasses mixed with pungent oil has not been consumed,
how could asthma be destroyed, O lady whose lips are sweet as nectar?
If powdered black pepper is consumed with honey and sugar, why worry? Cough and asthma are both conquered.
O Ratnakalā, whose eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus,
this decoction of *siṃhī* with *kaṇā* will instantly bring relief from coughing fits.
Cough is pacified by consuming long pepper, long pepper root, bibhitaka, and ginger with honey, even out of mere curiosity.
May the son of Rāvaṇa, supported by his lotus-like mouth, slay Śvasana or Kasana,
just as the son of Anila [Hanumān] did him.
O beloved of my life, O you with eyes as red as nutmeg!
One should have her drink a decoction prepared with ginger and bhāṅgī to alleviate her asthma.
O Lord of Life, my dearest friend Kandarpalīlā has now become exceedingly emaciated due to the affliction of consumption;
tell her the remedy for this, and let honey be given to her.
O lady with eyes like those of a cakora bird, take this powder made from viśvagranthi, kaṇā, and the fruit of the kalidruma tree.
This powder derived from the three pungents (trikaṭu), when combined with jaggery and ghee,
swiftly destroys coughs, just as Hari destroys the fears of the virtuous.
Whoever consumes the juice of ginger together with honey will never again have fear of asthma or cough.
Of him whose vehicle is the son of the father of the beloved of Pulomajā’s daughter,
and who has surpassed Rāma and Rāma [Kṛṣṇa] in beauty.
Astringent is the serpent of coughing wind.
A powder consisting of equal parts of triphalā, chinnaruhā, agni (citraka), rāsnā, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya) that destroy worms, combined with sugar.
One shall conquer cough; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
One should certainly drink pure castor oil alone, mixed with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) or mixed with a decoction of ginger (viśva), for pain in the waist, the flanks, and the bladder.
This decoction made from *rāsnā*, *amṛtā*, *nāgara*, *devadāru*, the five roots, the two pairs [of *śatāvarī*], and *indrayava*,
combined with *ruvūka* oil, [is effective].
He would become a breaker of the vital wind of raw flesh.
Just as a playful woman captivates the heart of a lover with her charm, so does guduchi remove undigested humors and wind from the entire body.

Kulattha beans grown in the forest, properly steamed and stripped of their husks by mature women, are bound in cloth and soaked in goat’s urine; then, ground finely at night, they are filled with the powder of pungent *rasa* and *niśā*.
Thrown into the eyes, they cause a transformation of the blood within three days.
The poet Lolimbarāja has described the application of this *śigru* tree as an ornament for women; what else could there be from its sap, which intoxicates even the bees?
O foremost among women, who removes the affliction of vision alone!
O lotus-eyed one, Kapha quickly renders Arjuna powerless along with the white [sugar],
just as a newly-wed bride renders her beloved husband impotent.
It was applied to the chest, which possessed small breasts.
Thus it has been declared by the Noble Ones that for those afflicted by eye diseases,
honey and the finest ghee should be consumed at night for the sake of comfort;
O you whose gaze is as tremulous as the playfulness of a young child, you are indeed the foremost [of such remedies].
Alas, why do you produce such extreme perversity?
Pippalī mixed with cow dung juice cures night-blindness,
just as a passionate woman dispels the great strength of her lover through sexual union.
O dark one, O not-dark one, O beloved dark one, O you whose mind is awakened by the dark!
[This] honey, when combined with honey, quickly pacifies the white [leprosy].
A decoction prepared from triphalā, vṛṣa, bhūnimba, nimba, tiktā, and amṛtā,
combined with honey and sugar, overcomes jaundice and anemia.
The juice of the *devadālī* fruit, when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), destroys jaundice;
of this there is no doubt, O lady with eyes like full-blown blue lotuses!
The collyrium of the mountain-born Atri, used for three nights, removes jaundice;
this shall not be false, for it is your own oath, O lady.
O slender one, with your charming earrings and your shimmering orb of a face-moon,
cow’s milk mixed with ginger cures jaundice.
A pill prepared from the seeds of *picumanda* (nimba), *anilaśatru* (musta), and mixed with the juice of *picumanda*, [should be placed] within the vagina.
One should wear it for the pacification of the pain of the female organ.
The root of the *uttaraṇī* plant combined with goat's ghee quickly destroys afflictions located in the womb known as "Śiva's weapon."
This decoction of gopī, vṛkī, dāru, kirāta, mūrvā, tiktā, amṛtā, viśva, ghana,
and indrajā is prescribed for women with deer-like eyes.
For the purification of corrupted milk.
A decoction made from the juices of *kaṭaṅkaṭerī*, *rasā* (liquorice), *abdavāsā* (musta), *bhūnimba*, *bhallī* (marking nut),
and sesame seeds, combined with honey, [is effective] for women of restless glances.
It cures various types of vaginal discharges.

O moon-faced one, this pair of medicines— the root of *taṇḍulīya* and that which is produced from juice— should be taken in equal parts with rice-water and honey by you whose eyes are like the petals of the blue water-lily.
It destroys the intense, gaping fissures of beautiful women.
The root of the gavākṣī plant, when placed in the temple of Love,
effects the destruction of the confinement of flowers for unfaithful women who have no husbands.
This very yoga [is effective] for causing an abortion in quick time.
Having drunk honey, ghee, liquorice, and the root of citron, Sumukhī gave birth easily;
[she who had consumed] a paste of white coriander with rice-water.
From drinking [this], vomiting occurs in pregnant women.

Mustā, śṛṅgī, and viṣāṇā— when consumed with honey, their pollen pacifies the afflictions caused by grains, years, oceans, the two [Ara]s, earth, nectar, poison, strength, and the dust of the wind; it is cool, difficult to touch, and cures the blood disorders, pain, diarrhea, and fever of pregnant women and those who have recently given birth.
Or for children, [one may give] the powder of *antikāsa* mixed with honey to treat fever caused by *ativiṣa*.
In cases of diarrhea in children, a decoction made from *samaṅgā*, *madāśārivā*, *rodhra*, and honey is beneficial; likewise,
[a decoction] of *madā*, *rodhra*, *bilva*, *abdam*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *vālā*.
Either a decoction or an electuary mixed with honey.
Fever and diarrhea are pacified by a powder made from equal parts of *kṛṣṇā*, *aruṇā*, *mustaka*, and *śṛṅgikā*, taken together with honey.
Accompanied by dyspnea, cough, and vomiting, it occurs in children.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vilāsinī Disease," in the *Vaidyajīvana* composed by Lolimbarāja, son of Śrī Divākara.
The fourth chapter: [Arising] from the playful speech of King Lolimba, the ornament of the learned.
O Lord, no satisfaction arises; please provide something more.
For the sake of destroying [defilements], producing [virtue], and bringing about liberation, let the Lion-faced One be constantly served;
O lotus-eyed one, trust has been placed in him by many.
O beautiful one, O lady with a lovely face and eyes with waves of charming outer corners,
from eating fresh butter, honey, and leaves...
There will be the destruction of the destruction of the moon-king.
O you who are enchanting with mālatī flowers shimmering amidst your rows of soft tresses!
This astringent decoction has been prepared from the three myrobalans.
Combined with *guggulu*, it conquers wounds.
At the time of dawn, while drinking cool water mixed with honey, [I am] the connoisseur named Madanajvarakārin, who possesses the jewel-like artistry of Rasa.
Even Gaṇanātha, it is said, would be reduced to nothing but bones.
A decoction prepared from the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), kaliṅga, nimba, trivṛt, ugrā, and khadira,
when drunk together with animal urine, [acts as a purgative].
Alas, it kills even millions of worms with its speed!
A decoction of *jātī*, *pravāla*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *yavāsa*, *dārvī*, *triyāmā*, *amṛtā*, and *gostanī*,
combined with honey, destroys [the disease].
The ripening of the face [is brought about] by that which resides in the lotus of the mouth.
In the midst of her pair of breasts, which are exceedingly delightful due to a shimmering, beautiful, and noble garland of mandāra flowers,
there is a mixture of turmeric powder and honey.
The decoction of śivā removes urinary disorders (prameha).
"O lady with a face like the autumn moon, all physicians declare that even when its juice is extracted, honey prevents various types of urinary disorders."
O you who are skilled in the arts of amorous play, whose bracelets shimmer, and whose breasts are like Mount Malaya;
[this is] the nectar-creeper mixed with *ruvu* oil.
He checked the exceedingly violent flow of his wind-blood.
Piṇḍataila, boiled with the smoke of cowherd women who are as ruddy as honey, cures vātarakta; likewise,
a decoction drunk with castor oil [is effective].
Likewise for the castor-oil plant, the lion-mouthed plant, and the vatsādanī.
This powder, consisting of equal parts of garlic, cumin, sulphur, rock salt, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), and asafoetida,
immediately cures cholera when taken with the juice of lime.
O you who are skilled in the enjoyment of delight, take it!
A pill prepared with *ruglāja*, *abdarohā*, *vaṭapraroha*, and *madhuka*, mixed with honey, when held within the mouth,
quickly and thoroughly pacifies even severe thirst. [Likewise, a pill made of] *elā*, *lāja*, *lavaṅga*, *nāga*, *capalā*, *śrīkola* pith, and *ambuda*...
Sandalwood combined with jaggery relieves vomiting arising from the three doṣas.
O you whose form is delightful like Ramā, whose speech is clever, whose locks of hair are beautiful, who have cast aside ornaments, and in whose palm a blue lotus shines—
has the summer truly arisen for you, or is it merely the birth of a lotus and the ripening of a plantain?
O you who are skilled in literature, sleep lightly upon this bed prepared with cotton wool.
Of these— rasa, dvijīra, the two types of niśā, marīca, sindūra, daityendra, and manaḥśilā—
having been powdered and mixed with ghee, [one should take one karṣa daily].
Pāmā departs by means of three medicinal plasters.
A bolus (modaka) made from equal parts of harītakī, sesame seeds, and *āruṣkara* combined with jaggery cures hemorrhoids,
anemia, fever, skin diseases, and cough.
One should likewise conquer dyspnea and the disease of the spleen.
By anointing both feet with a paste of madana, saindhava salt, guggulu, red ochre, clarified butter, honey, and vālaka, even if they were entirely cracked, [they would become whole].
It would become like a blossoming *tāmarasa* lotus.
By applying a plaster composed of the roots of *bhallātaka*, *asīsa*, *hutāśa*, and *dantī*, smeared with molasses, *snuhī* latex, and cow's milk,
a chain of glandular swellings (*gaṇḍamālā*) is cured.
Like a mass of clouds driven by the force of the wind.
A decoction made from bhūnimba, nimba, triphalā, paṭola, vāsā, amṛtā, parpaṭa, and bhṛṅgarāja,
when combined with honey, removes amlapitta.
The mind is like the sidelong glance of a courtesan.
Asafoetida, the two types of alkali, rock salt, black salt, biḍa salt, long pepper, granthika, citraka, cavya, black pepper, carcūra, cumin, barbarī, tamarind,
ṣaḍgranthā, ajamodā, amlavetasa, puṣkaramūla, ginger, and karañja—
This powder, prepared with *jīraka*, *harītakī*, *vṛkī*, and *hapuṣā*, [cures] urinary calculi,
diseases of the heart and throat, constipation, flatulence, hiccups, abdominal distension, hemorrhoids, tumors, all types of colic, splenic disorders, anemia, asthma, cough, and burning sensations.
It is more effective for the cessation of the distaste arising from constant speaking and silence.

A decoction made with cow’s urine of *kaliṅga*, *kaṭukā*, *pāṭhā*, *vṛṣa*, *abda*, *amara*, mixed with honey, destroys all severe diseases of the throat. [Likewise, a preparation of] *pāṭhā*, *tejovatī*, *rasāñjana*, *yavakṣāra*, *upakulyā*, and *niśā*— [The remainder of the verse follows: —mixed with honey, destroys all severe diseases of the throat. Just as honey is placed upon the mouths of the gods, so too does this pill remain.
"O lord of my life, O most beloved, tell me what I should say; O lover, what indeed, O deer-eyed one, would cause pain?
"Listen well, O affectionate one; I am listening to you, my dear."
He should eat it with the juice of citron, rock salt, and ginger.
One should first consume asafoetida, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), ajamoda, dvijaraṇa, and salt with ghee;
this, when eaten, makes the fire blaze intensely and destroys abdominal tumors born of wind (vātagulma).
Likewise, vṛkṣāmla, amlavetasa, agni, pathyā, the three pungents, viḍa salt, jantuja, and the two types of jīraka [achieve the same].
It sets ablaze even refined borax and reduces even a mountain entirely to ashes.
Five parts of ginger, four parts of long pepper,

three parts of *dīpyaka* (cumin), two parts of *yavānī*, and one part of salt— this [mixture] equal to the number of Śiva (eleven) is declared by Lolimbarāja as a remedy for distension of the abdomen, pain, undigested matter (*āmadoṣa*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and disorders of the feces.
Powder reduces even mountains to ashes; what need be said, O people, of food?
A decoction made from *śigru*, *dīpya*, *varuṇa*, *ativiṣā*, *yāminī*, and *kuñjarāśana*,
combined with powdered *bola*, [cures] that which has arisen internally.
One will undoubtedly burst open an abscess.
O you who are enchanting with a necklace resting upon a pair of breasts resembling lotus buds—
Arjuna has offered clarified butter as a remedy for the diseases of the heart.
Well-prepared with its own juice and paste, O lady!
Thus this Bakula tree, with its fragrant buds, shines forth as the foremost of trees, O dearest one, the sole kinsman of the god of love;
by whose very bark, when long-chewed, [the mouth becomes] exceedingly...
Even though their teeth are fickle, they become like diamonds.
Who breaks the temple-front of an elephant?

What does a newlywed bride say when she is impassioned? What is the vocative for "us"? And what is *raktapitta*? [The answers are: *kumbha* (the frontal globe), *avyayam* (an indeclinable), *rate* (O husband!), and *nuḥ* (the suffix *nu*).
O lady with beautiful thighs, speak yourself; it destroys [the enemy].

The powder of *viśvāśiva* (dry ginger) and *kaṇā* (long pepper), combined with sugar and honey, is prescribed as a nasal drop (*nasya*); likewise, a preparation of *viśva* and jaggery (*guḍa*) is known to be a formidable suppressor of hiccup.
By the consumption of a decoction of *durālabhā* mixed with clarified butter,
dizziness is pacified, just as sin is removed by the remembrance of Govinda.
O jewel-like girl, do not engage in quarreling,
O you whose gait is like that of a female swan;
listen to my words and speak, O gem among physicians.
O lady with intoxicating eyes, may wine allay my grief.
A decoction of punarnavā, nāgara, dāru, pathyā, bhallātaka, and chinnaruhā,
combined with ten parts of sugar, should be drunk for [the treatment of] the thighs.
Or else, there is the application of urine and feces to a pillar.
One who regularly consumes *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *gokṣura*, *śivā*, *śamyāka*, *pāṣāṇabhida*, and *duḥsparśa* with honey will immediately eliminate even difficult-to-overcome urinary calculi (*aśmarī*).
Furthermore, a powder of *elā*, *parvata-bhitt* (rock salt), *śilājatu*, and *kaṇā*, combined with jaggery, [achieves the same].
When drunk with rice-washing water, it removes dysuria.

A decoction made from *vāsā*, *elā*, *madhuka*, *aśmabheda*, *capalā*, *kauntī*, *kṣura*, and *eraṇḍa*, combined with *aśmajatu*, greatly overcomes difficult urination (*kṛcchra*), urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), and gravel (*śarkarā*).
For painful urination accompanied by burning sensations and constipation, a decoction of *aśmabhid* and *gokṣura* [is recommended].
A preparation made from *nanta*, *āragvadha*, and *cetakī*, combined with honey, is recommended.

An ointment for rubbing the body (*udvartana*), prepared from *nyagrodha* sprouts, *kuṣṭha*, *lodhra*, *vikasā*, *śyāmā*, *masūra*, *aruṇa*, and *śrīkhaṇḍa* mixed with milk, destroys freckles (*vyaṅga*). Alternatively, one may be smeared with the powder of *masūra* along with ghee, milk, and rice for seven days.
The face of Vyaṅga would become more beautiful than the autumnal moon through its transformation.

A paste of the pulp of *iṅgudī* fruit mixed with water, when applied to the face, bestows beauty; likewise, *rodhra*, *ugrā*, and *dhanikā*, when used as a facial application, destroy pimples born of youth.
